newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian decrees seen right step to monopoly reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian decrees seen right step to monopoly reform.

text.p: Reformist First Deputy Premier Boris Nemtsov announced decrees on Monday which economists say will consolidate his power and set Russia's largest companies on the road to efficiency.

Nemtsov said the presidential decrees would strengthen the government's regulatory role in natural monopolies, large companies without competitors such as electricity and natural gas producers, telecoms and railways.

The economists said Nemtsov, a young liberal brought into the government from a regional governorship last month, was correct to increase the state's role in corporate governance. Nemtsov heads the drive to squeeze the monopolies' bloated bureaucracies.
"In this situation you have very strong control by reformers at the top level, which means (they) can start working," said Brunswick brokerage research director Per Maelstrom.

"But it comes down to politics because the biggest problems are going to be at the regional level," he said. Essential federal reforms would take about six months and regions would be in the process for a couple of years.
The International Monetary Fund and foreign investors have said Russia needs a new tax code and improved corporate transparency and efficiency in its natural monopolies.

Nemtsov said Gazprom, which produces 94 percent of Russia's natural gas, and Unified Energy System (UES), which generates power and has controlling stakes in most local regional power utilities, would remain single, state-controlled companies.
But he said oil companies which must sell their natural gas to Gazprom would be given equal access to the company's pipelines and rights to new gas deposits would be auctioned.

The Federal Energy Commission, under control of the liberal Economy Ministry and the Fuel and Energy Ministry, which Nemtsov also heads, will set tariffs for UES's national power grid, which he said needed to be expanded.
Nemtsov said the grid needed $8 billion investment in the short term and that independent power utilities and consumers would have direct access to the grid.

"After a single energy system is formed as truly one company, not like now, and after generating companies become incorporated, we could talk about a competitive environment in which the role of private capital could increase and that of the government decrease," Nemtsov told a news conference.
He said Gazprom, UES and local utilities and telecoms companies would all need investment capital. Supporting Gazprom's share price was a major reform goal, he said.
CentreInvest research chief James Fenkner said Western investors were ready to absorb securities from the monopolies.
UES has said it is planning to issue American Depositary Receipts (ADR), share look-alikes that trade on foreign markets.
Gazprom plans a second ADR and 25 percent of telecom holding company Svyazinvest will also be open for bidding to foreign and domestic investors next month.
But Fenkner said the new decree would not necessarily change the market. "This decree is a comfort factor, but I don't know if it is the (trigger) point at which you buy or sell."
A Western diplomat said the changes were a good first step but that investors were looking for broader moves.

"(Investors) are going to look for more than monopolies," the diplomat said. "Foreign companies want to work in a transparent environment, but they will want tax reform and rule of law before the big money begins coming here.
"Hopefully changing the way key monopolies operate will convince companies they need to change the way they operate," the diplomat said. "It is a signal that will be sent through the system."
